claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the ability to form a stable, self-healing multicomponent passive oxide layer.
A stable multicomponent passive oxide layer shields the alloy surface from mechanical damage.
A stable multicomponent passive oxide layer shields the alloy surface from corrosive attack.
The proposed test alloy begins with a homogeneous, well-annealed microstructure.
The proposed test alloy begins with a uniformly polished surface free of pre-existing damage.
Diverse elemental composition in high-entropy alloys promotes rapid formation and self-healing of a multicomponent oxide film.
Inherent lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys promotes rapid formation and self-healing of a multicomponent oxide film.
The multicomponent oxide film reduces direct exposure of the substrate to the environment.
The multicomponent oxide film rapidly regenerates after mechanical damage.
Enhancing oxide-layer formation will reduce overall mass loss relative to a matched baseline lacking the proposed compositional advantages.
Enhancing oxide-layer formation will produce shallower wear scars relative to the matched baseline.
Enhancing oxide-layer formation will lower corrosion current density relative to the matched baseline.
The baseline should have mechanical properties similar to those of the oxide-optimized alloy while lacking the optimized passive-film-forming composition.
The prediction is expected to hold under moderate corrosive and mechanical conditions.
The prediction may fail at very high or very low pH because such environments can compromise oxide stability.
The prediction may fail under severe mechanical loads that disrupt oxide stability.
The quantitative reduction in degradation may vary with environmental severity and the exact compositional modification.
A controlled comparison can test the hypothesis by subjecting an oxide-optimized high-entropy alloy and a mechanically matched baseline to identical cyclic sliding in corrosive saline solution.
Failure of the optimized alloy to improve mass loss, wear-scar depth, and corrosion current density, together with absence of a stable self-healing oxide film, would falsify the hypothesis.
